Transformer models trained on large corpora have transformed natural language processing, yet they fail on systematic compositional tasks: a model that learns "blue circle" and "red square" rarely generalises to "red circle" without explicit training. We identify this as a data-coverage problem, not a model-capacity problem.

We introduce Compositional Augmentation (CompAug), a data synthesis method that generates compositional examples from atomic phrase embeddings during fine-tuning. On the SCAN benchmark, CompAug raises exact-match accuracy from 61.4% to 89.3% with no change to model architecture. On COGS, it closes 78% of the compositional generalisation gap.

Three findings stand out. First, the gain is largest on length-generalisation splits (17.2 points), smaller on structural splits (8.4 points), and smallest on lexical splits (3.1 points). Second, augmentation during fine-tuning outperforms augmentation during pretraining by 6.1 points, suggesting that task-specific composition patterns are learned late. Third, CompAug degrades by 2.3 points when the atomic phrase vocabulary exceeds 50k tokens; we trace this to embedding-space crowding and propose a nearest-neighbour filtering step that recovers 1.9 of those points.

These results suggest that systematic generalisation failures in large language models are partly addressable through targeted training data rather than architectural changes—a cheaper intervention with broad practical implications.
